lesson.title: Ida Tarbell and the Twenty-Year Case Against Standard Oil
lesson.summary: Ida Tarbell's meticulously documented History of the Standard Oil Company, serialized in McClure's Magazine from 1902 to 1904, exposed how John D. Rockefeller built his oil monopoly through secret railroad rebates and predatory tactics, and helped build the public and legal case that broke the company apart in 1911.
lesson.body:
Ida Tarbell grew up in the oil regions of northwestern Pennsylvania, where her father worked in the oil business during the years Standard Oil, led by John D. Rockefeller, was consolidating control over the American petroleum industry. Tarbell watched Standard Oil's practices squeeze independent producers like her father out of the market, and that early exposure shaped the project she would eventually undertake as a journalist for McClure's Magazine.

Starting in 1902, Tarbell published a serialized investigation eventually collected as The History of the Standard Oil Company. Rather than relying on outrage or anecdote, she built her case out of court records, corporate documents, and interviews, tracing in careful detail how Rockefeller's company had grown from a Cleveland refinery into a monopoly controlling the great majority of American oil refining. She documented how Standard Oil had secured secret rebates from railroads, a practice that let it ship oil more cheaply than competitors and effectively let the railroads help crush rivals, and how it used predatory pricing, industrial espionage, and pressure on suppliers to absorb or eliminate competitors. Her reporting was distinctive for its restraint and precision, treating readers as capable of following a long, complex financial argument rather than needing to be told what to feel.

Tarbell's work landed at a moment when the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 had gone largely unenforced, and it gave both the public and government prosecutors a detailed roadmap of exactly how a monopoly like Standard Oil had been assembled. Her reporting became part of the evidentiary and political groundwork behind the federal antitrust case against Standard Oil, which culminated in the Supreme Court's 1911 decision in Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, ordering the company broken into more than thirty separate companies. That case unfolded under President Taft rather than Theodore Roosevelt, but it belonged to the broader trust-busting climate Roosevelt's presidency had done so much to create.

Tarbell's career also complicates a common assumption about the muckrakers, since she did not consider herself a radical and was skeptical of some Progressive proposals, including women's suffrage. What made her book so effective was not ideology but method: exhaustive documentation aimed at a single, powerful target, showing that a journalist with enough patience could hold even the wealthiest man in America accountable in public.
